components.gap: Supply the source's claims that motivate this entry's hypothesis, and the hypothesis as printed (Durrett pp. 214-215). First, regular conditional distributions do not always exist: the first example is due to Dieudonne (1948), with Doob (1953), p. 624, and Faden (1985) for later developments, and the difficulty is that each countable-additivity identity for conditional probabilities holds only outside its own null set, so that when S has enough countable disjoint collections the exceptional sets may pile up. Second, Theorem 4.1.17 assumes (S, S) nice, which its proof unpacks as a one-to-one map phi from S into R with phi and its inverse measurable, with no clause that phi(S) is Borel. The routed theorem (regular-conditional-laws.tex lines 95-110; annex lines 139-181) assumes a measurable isomorphism onto a Borel set and says only that it makes the source's image and concentration requirements explicit; the route neither states the nonexistence claim with its attributions and mechanism (lines 41 and 254-256 say only that exceptional sets can depend on the event and that existence is not asserted for every space) nor settles the status of Theorem 4.1.17 under the hypothesis as printed.
